From Wiktionary, the free dictionary

English

[edit]

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /ˈspiːʃi/, /ˈspiːsi/
    • Audio (Southern England):(file)
    • Rhymes: -iːʃi, -iːsi
  • (obsolete) IPA(key): /ˈspiːʃiː/, /ˈspiːʃi.iː/[1][2]

Etymology 1

[edit]

Originally in the phrase in specie; from Latin speciē, ablative singular of species. Compare in kind.

Noun

[edit]

specie (uncountable)

  1. Type or kind, in various uses of the phrase in specie.
  2. Money in the form of coins made from precious metal that has an intrinsic value; coinage.
    Antonym: paper
    • 1830, Joseph Plumb Martin, “Ch. IX”, in A Narrative of Some of the Adventures, Dangers and Sufferings of a Revolutionary Soldier:
      I received one month's pay in specie while on the march to Virginia, in the year 1781, and except that, I never received any pay worth the name while I belonged to the army.
    • 1982, Lawrence Durrell, Constance (Avignon Quintet), Faber & Faber, published 2004, page 805:
      ‘It was not money or specie he thought himself hunting!’
    • 2006, Thomas Pynchon, Against the Day, Vintage, published 2007, page 8:
      “Dick” Counterfly had absquatulated swiftly into the night, leaving his son with only a pocketful of specie and the tender admonition, “Got to ‘scram,’ kid — write if you get work.”
Derived terms
[edit]
  • specie point
Related terms
[edit]
  • sub specie aeterni
Translations
[edit]
classification
  • Esperanto: specio (eo), speco (eo)
money
  • Bulgarian: монети (bg) f pl (moneti)
  • Catalan: espècie (ca) f
  • Danish: specie c
  • Finnish: raha (fi)
  • Manx: argid meainey m

See also

[edit]
  • payment in kind

Etymology 2

[edit]

Back-formation from species (plural), the final “s” being misinterpreted as a plural ending.

Noun

[edit]

specie (plural species)

  1. (hypercorrect) singular of species
Usage notes
[edit]
  • Although in wide use, this is universally considered by prescriptive references to be an error.

References

[edit]
  1. ^ Michaelis, Hermann; Jones, Daniel (1913), “'spiːʃiː”, in A Phonetic Dictionary of the English Language (Sammlung Phonetischer Wörterbücher; 2)‎[1], Hanover: Carl Meyer (Gustav Prior), →OCLC, page 392: “[-iiː]”
  2. ^ James A. H. Murray et al., editors (1884–1928), “Specie”, in A New English Dictionary on Historical Principles (Oxford English Dictionary), volume IX, Part 1 (Si–St), London: Clarendon Press, →OCLC, page 545, column 3: “spī·ʃi, spī·ʃī, spī·ʃiī”

Anagrams

[edit]
  • pieces

Dutch

[edit]

Etymology

[edit]

From Middle Dutch specie (“kind, sort”, 14th c.), borrowed from Latin speciēs. The sense “mortar” also appears in spijs, Middle Dutch spise (literally “food”), and it is not clear which of the two words developed it first; compare German Speis, Maurerspeise.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /ˈspeː.si/
  • Audio:(file)
  • Hyphenation: spe‧cie
  • Rhymes: -eːsi

Noun

[edit]

specie f (plural speciën or species, no diminutive)

  1. mortar (mixture of lime or cement, sand and water)
    Synonyms: metselspecie, mortel
  2. material used in casting
  3. coinage, specie, coins

Derived terms

[edit]
  • metselspecie

Descendants

[edit]
  • → Indonesian: spesi

Italian

[edit]
Italian Wikipedia has an article on:
specie
Wikipedia it

Etymology

[edit]

Borrowed from Latin speciēs. Doublet of spezie.

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • IPA(key): /ˈspɛ.t͡ʃe/
  • Audio (IT):(file)
  • Rhymes: -ɛtʃe
  • Hyphenation: spè‧cie

Adverb

[edit]

specie

  1. especially, particularly
    Nonostante la sua abilità, Clemens ha avuto poca fama, specie tra i suoi contemporanei.
    Despite his ability, Clemens had little fame, particularly among his contemporaries.

Noun

[edit]

specie f (invariable)

  1. kind, type, sort
  2. (biology) species, strain, breed
  3. (taxonomy) species

Derived terms

[edit]
  • fare specie (“to amaze, shock”)

Related terms

[edit]
  • cronospecie
  • speciale
  • speciazione
  • specifico

Latin

[edit]

Pronunciation

[edit]
  • (Classical Latin) IPA(key): [ˈspɛ.ki.eː]
  • (modern Italianate Ecclesiastical) IPA(key): [ˈspɛː.t͡ʃi.e]

Noun

[edit]

speciē

  1. ablative singular of speciēs

Preposition

[edit]

speciē (+ genitive)

  1. under the pretext of; under the guise of

References

[edit]
  • “specie”, in Gaffiot, Félix (1934), Dictionnaire illustré latin-français, Hachette.
  • Carl Meißner; Henry William Auden (1894), Latin Phrase-Book‎[2], London: Macmillan and Co.
    • (ambiguous) in truth; really: re (vera), reapse (opp. specie)
    • (ambiguous) apparently; to look at: specie (De Amic. 13. 47)

Etymology

Borrowed from Latin speciēs.

specie f (plural specii)

  1. (biology) species
  2. kind, type, sort
